pharm: A low-potency topical glucocorticoid with anti-inflammatory, antipruritic and vasoconstrictive activity, used to relieve inflammation and itching in corticosteroid-responsive skin conditions

summary: Desonide cream 0.05% is a low-potency topical corticosteroid indicated for relief of the inflammatory and pruritic manifestations of corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses (such as atopic dermatitis/eczema). It is applied as a thin film to the affected area two to four times daily and, like other topical steroids, is discontinued once control is achieved. It should not be used for longer than two weeks unless directed by a physician and should not be used with occlusive dressings. Extensive application, occlusion or prolonged use can cause sufficient systemic absorption to suppress the HPA axis - a particular concern in children, who have a higher skin-surface-to-body-mass ratio.

moa: Like other topical corticosteroids, desonide has anti-inflammatory, antipruritic and vasoconstrictive properties. Although the exact mechanism is unclear, corticosteroids are thought to induce phospholipase A2-inhibitory proteins (lipocortins) that reduce the release of arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids, thereby suppressing the synthesis of inflammatory mediators such as prostaglandins and leukotrienes.

Application to thin or inflamed skin or to the face/intertriginous areas (enhanced absorption)

preg: Corticosteroids are teratogenic in laboratory animals when given systemically at relatively low doses, and some are teratogenic after dermal application in animals; reproduction studies have not been conducted with desonide cream and there are no adequate, well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus, applying the smallest amount for the shortest time.
lact: Systemically administered corticosteroids appear in human milk; it is not known whether topical application produces sufficient systemic absorption to yield detectable amounts in milk. Because many drugs are excreted in human milk, use caution when administering to a nursing woman and avoid applying to the breast/nipple area before nursing.
renal: No specific topical dosage adjustment is described for renal impairment.
hepatic: No specific topical dosage adjustment is described for hepatic impairment.

pearls: Desonide is a low-potency topical corticosteroid suited to atopic dermatitis/eczema and to thin or sensitive skin areas
Limit use to 2 weeks unless directed and discontinue once control is achieved to minimise local and systemic effects
Do not use under occlusive dressings - occlusion markedly increases percutaneous absorption and systemic risk
Children are at greater risk of HPA-axis suppression, Cushing's syndrome, growth retardation and intracranial hypertension because of their higher skin-surface-to-body-mass ratio - use minimally
Local adverse effects (atrophy, striae, folliculitis, perioral dermatitis) occur more often with potent steroids, occlusion and prolonged use
If there is no improvement within 2 weeks, reassess the diagnosis
missed: If a dose is missed, apply it when remembered. If it is almost time for the next application, skip the missed dose and resume the usual schedule - do not apply extra to make up for a missed dose.
overdose: Topically applied desonide can be absorbed in sufficient amounts to produce systemic corticosteroid effects, particularly with extensive application, occlusion or prolonged use. Excessive or prolonged use can lead to HPA-axis suppression with features of hypercortisolism (Cushing's syndrome), hyperglycaemia and glycosuria. Manage by reducing the frequency, withdrawing the corticosteroid (gradually if used extensively/long term to avoid acute adrenal insufficiency) and providing supportive care; treat local reactions appropriately.
